MATH 237: Foundations of Data Science¶

Project 1: Spotify Tracks Dataset¶

Group Members: Jonathan Brennan, Summer Bui, Rakif Nassif, Jasmine Pena, Daniel Sillas

For our first MATH 237 project, we chose one of 3 offered datasets, the Spotify Tracks dataset. We use this dataset to conduct exploratory analysis and attempt to uncover any interesting information based on the data provided.

Spotify Tracks Dataset:

  • 73609 unique tracks covering 114 different genres
  • Data collected using Spotify API and Python
  • Measurements provided

Data Source: Maharshi Pandya, Spotify Tracks Dataset (2022).

Documentation: https://doi.org/10.34740/kaggle/dsv/4372070

Project Objective¶

Our group will demonstrate our ability to apply course learnings to a real-world dataset. Skills demonstrated within this project involve:

  • Using given information within our dataset to create direction
  • Hypothesize and conduct conceivable research questions for exploration
  • Select and cleanly visualize graphs/tables to efficiently explore our research questions
  • Cautiously approach data to showcase ethical consideration
  • Collaborate with team members to complete project by a given due date

Introduction¶

Our group chose to explore the Spotify dataset. Within this dataset, there are 114 genres. We focused on the top 5 genres. These include: pop/film, kpop, chill, sad, and grunge. We wanted to investigate and determine what features define a genre, and what separates popular from unpopular songs within a genre. Looking at these genres, what makes each of them unique? As previosuly mentioned, there are 114 genres within the dataset. Each genre includes 1,000 songs. Overall, there are 114,000 songs in the dataset. Initially, we each explored all the features for each of our genres. From there, we each decided which features have the strongest correlations for our genre. Daniel did Pop/Film. Jasmine did Chill. Jonathan did Grunge. Rafik did Kpop. Summer did Sad.

Brief variable descriptions¶

  • track_id: The Spotify ID for the track
  • artists: The name of the artist of the track. Multiple artists are separated with a ;
  • album_name: The name of the track's album
  • track_name: The name of the track
  • popularity: The popularity of the track (0-100), based mostly on number of plays a track has
  • duration_ms: The length of the track in milliseconds (ms).
  • explicit: Whether or not a track has explicit language (true = yes, false = no)
  • danceability: How suitable the track is for dancing (0.00-1.00). Measured using various song features
  • energy: How much measured intensity/activity (0.00-1.00) is within a track. Measured through BPM, loudness, and noisiness.
  • key: The key the track is in. Mapped using standard Pitch Class notation (ex. 0 = C, 1 = C♯/D♭, 2 = D).
  • loudness: The loudness of a track in decibels (dB).
  • mode: The modality of a track (major/minor). Major = 1 and minor = 0.
  • speechiness: The presence of spoken words in a track (0.00-1.00). Measured by how exclusively "speechy" it is (ex. a podcast would have high speechiness).
  • acousticness: A confidence measure of whether or not the track is acoustic (0.00-1.00).
  • instrumentalness: A measure predicting whether or not a track contains no vocals (0.00-1.00).
  • liveness: A measure predicting whether or not there was a live audience (0.00-1.00). Measured through detection of audience.
  • valence: The measurement describing musical positiveness within the track (0.00-1.00).
  • tempo: The estimated tempo of a track (BPM).
  • time_signature: The estimated time signature of a track (ex. 3 = 3/4).
  • track_genre: The genre of a track. Tracks can have more than one genre and are provided as duplicates in the dataset.

Research Questions¶

After briefly exploring our dataset, we chose 4 research questions to base our exploratory analysis on:

  1. What aspects of songs affect its popularity?
  2. What contributes to the valence of a track?
  3. What features are associated with the top 5 genres?
  4. What are the unique characteristics of the top 5 genres in relation to popularity?

Within the dataset's variable description, it states:

For keys: Mapped integers follow standard Pitch Class notation.

NOTE: The variable description of time_signature does not match the values we're given. We don't want to misrepresent the data, so we'll leave the values as is.

Let's create mappings for both our keys and nodes variables to turn the integers into an object datatype. We can use this to better clarify what each integer represents.

In [69]:
# Mapping out new columns
key_mapping = {
    0 : "C",
    1 : "C♯/D♭",
    2 : "D",
    3 : "D♯/E♭",
    4 : "E",
    5 : "F",
    6 : "F♯/G♭",
    7 : "G",
    8 : "G♯/A♭",
    9 : "A",
    10 : "A♯/B♭",
    11 : "B"
}

mode_mapping = {
    0 : "Minor",
    1 : "Major"
}

# Applying our mappings to new features
spotify['key_string'] = spotify['key'].map(key_mapping)
spotify['mode_string'] = spotify['mode'].map(mode_mapping)

# Printing out the new and old variables side-by-side to better represent the product of the
# mapping and encoding process
print("Key values encoded:")
key_comparison = spotify[['key', 'key_string']].drop_duplicates().sort_values('key')
print(key_comparison)
print("\nMode values encoded:")
mode_comparison = spotify[['mode', 'mode_string']].drop_duplicates().sort_values('mode')
print(mode_comparison)

RESEARCH QUESTION 1: What aspects of songs affect its popularity?¶

Our first research question deals with popularity. We want to examine the features through both a correlation matrix and within created popularity bins to see if there are any distinct features that stand out between groups.

Correlation Matrix¶

We used a correlation matrix before other exploratory approaches to see if there are significant correlations we can spot.

popularity_correlations = spotify_top5[popularity_vars].corr().round(2)

print(popularity_correlations)

Binning¶

We will bin the feature popularity to further examine the relationship of features across groupings. It is also done to turn it into categorical data, allowing us to examine it in ways other than correlation matrices. To bin our data, we'll first examine the distribution of popularity to determine how bins should be made.

In [78]:
# Popularity
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.hist(spotify_top5['popularity'], bins=45, color='skyblue', alpha=0.7, edgecolor='black')
plt.title('Distribution of Popularity Across Songs', fontsize=16)
plt.xlabel('Popularity', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Number of Responses', fontsize=12)
plt.xticks(np.arange(0, 100, 5))
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

# Pick the bins based on mode
# Or maybe investigate the outlier in 0 based on features of the artists in 0...
# maybe they only have a couple songs in Spotify? Don't rush to delete just

Observation: The spread of the popularity seems to be bimodal with a lot of outliers that are ranked between 0 and 5.

Before we bin popularity:

  • There is a large amount of outliers between 0 and 5. We're going to bin the lower ratings (0-19) to investigate these values.
  • The data appears to be bimodal. We're going to bin (20-44) and (45-66) to represent and investigate these modes.
  • We will bin the right of the rightmost mode (67-100) to represent and investigate popular tracks while attempting to keep sample size high.
In [79]:
# Binning popularity
spotify_top5 = spotify_top5.copy()

spotify_top5['popularity_group'] = pd.cut(spotify_top5['popularity'],
                                          bins=[0, 19, 44, 66, np.inf],
                                          labels=['Very Unpopular', 'Unpopular', 'Popular', 'Very Popular'],
                                          include_lowest=True)

# Reporting new features
print(f"New feature created:")
popularity_comparison = spotify_top5[['popularity', 'popularity_group']].drop_duplicates()
print(popularity_comparison)

# Counting the # of values in each group
print("Popularity distribution across tracks:")
print(spotify_top5["popularity_group"].value_counts())

OBSERVATION: Moving onward, we should be cautious when examining data using our popularity binnings. Popular tracks has a much larger sample size (n = 3520) than the rest of the binnings. Also, very unpopular tracks are smaller (n = 205) than other binnings.

Boolean Masks¶

We're going to create a boolean mask to compare categorical data. Some features, mainly key, have too many categories and will become too hard to read if we attempt to graph on a single graph.

In [80]:
# Boolean masking based on popularity group
track_verypopular = spotify_top5[spotify_top5['popularity_group'] == 'Very Popular']
track_popular = spotify_top5[spotify_top5['popularity_group'] == 'Popular']
track_unpopular = spotify_top5[spotify_top5['popularity_group'] == 'Unpopular']
track_veryunpopular = spotify_top5[spotify_top5['popularity_group'] == 'Very Unpopular']

Categorical data¶

I will use a crosstabulation to present the percentages of categorical data within popularity binnings. I do this because there is an unproportionate amount of people within the popular binning; showing the count would not help visualize the information being represented. Using percentages helps communicate our information. The crosstabulation results are represented through a heatmap plot to visualize the results of our methods to the viewer.

Key-Mode-Explicit Visualization¶

In [81]:
# A visualization of our crosstabs
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(18, 12))

# Making separate values for our crosstabs
pop_key_ct = pd.crosstab(spotify_top5['popularity_group'], spotify_top5['key_string'], normalize='index')\
.round(4)*100
pop_mode_ct = pd.crosstab(spotify_top5['popularity_group'], spotify_top5['mode_string'], normalize='index')\
.round(4)*100
pop_exp_ct = pd.crosstab(spotify_top5['popularity_group'], spotify_top5['explicit'], normalize='index')\
.round(4)*100

# Creating heatmaps from our crosstabs
sns.heatmap(pop_key_ct, annot=True, cmap='YlOrRd', ax=axes[0,0])
axes[0,0].set_title('Popularity Group-Key Crosstab by Percentage')
axes[0,0].set_xlabel('Key')
axes[0,0].set_ylabel('Popularity Group')

sns.heatmap(pop_mode_ct, annot=True, cmap='YlOrRd', ax=axes[0,1])
axes[0,1].set_title('Popularity Group-Mode Crosstab by Percentage')
axes[0,1].set_xlabel('Mode')
axes[0,1].set_ylabel('Popularity Group')

sns.heatmap(pop_exp_ct, annot=True, cmap='YlOrRd', ax=axes[1,0])
axes[1,0].set_title('Popularity Group-Explicit Crosstab by Percentage')
axes[1,0].set_xlabel('Explicit')
axes[1,0].set_ylabel('Popularity Group')

plt.suptitle('Heatmaps of Key-Mode-Explicit Crosstab Results')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations:

Popularity: There are changes in percentage of key usage across popularity groups.

  • A is more frequent in very unpopular/unpopular group
  • A♯/B♭ is more frequent in very popular/popular group
  • C is less frequent in very popular group
  • F♯/G♭ is less frequent in very unpopular group
  • There's noticeable variance across groups in G♯/A♭ and F

Modality: The unpopular and very unpopular binnings have a higher percentage of songs in major than the popular and very popular binnings.

Explicity: A higher percentage of songs within the very unpopular binning are recorded as explicit.

Numerical Values¶

We will utilize both a mean comparison table and boxplots of our desired variables to examine the relationship of features across popularity binnings. Means help us distinguish between averages amongst groups while boxplots provide an efficient method of comparison across group spreads.

Conclusion¶

We used several forms of summary and graph analyze to examine the relationship of features in relation to popularity. We used bins to create popularity "groups" to examine.

There were several findings we observed. To be specific:

  2. There was proportional difference amongst categorical variables key, mode, and explicit.

RESEARCH QUESTION 2: What contributes to the valence of a track?¶

When examining the variables featured within the dataset, we became concerned with how valence was measured. We aim to seek for correlations between valence and other features explored within the dataset. We will use a correlation matrix to examine features, then use a scatterplot to determine correlationship between specific features.

Correlation Matrix¶

We're creating a correlation matrix to examine the relationships of all features and see if there are any relationships worth further examining:

In [84]:
# Calculate correlations between body measurements
valence_vars = ['valence', 'mode', 'energy', 'tempo', 'danceability', 'speechiness', 'acousticness', 'instrumentalness', 'liveness', 'loudness']
valence_correlations = spotify_top5[valence_vars].corr().round(2)

print("Correlations between track features:")
print(valence_correlations)

Observations: There are weak correlations to valence within features loudness, energy, and danceability. Previously observed correlations within instrumentalness, acousticness, and speechiness seem to be due to a large amount of values being placed near 0; therefore, it is hard to determine if this relationship is informative.

Conclusion¶

Using both a correlation matrix and scatterplots, we found weak, positive correlations to valence in features:

  • Loudness
  • Energy
  • Danceability

Other correlations were observed, but informative data gained is questionable due to how the data is represented within the scatterplot.

RESEARCH QUESTION 3: What are the unique features of each of the 5 selected genres?¶

We aim to examine how each one of our five chosen genre's features differ amongst others. We will use similar methods as Research Question 1 to produce results, as both questions examine across groupings.

Categorical Data¶

We will use a crosstab to examine proportional differences in key, modality, and explicity across genres. When using a crosstab, the values given on the heatmap are percentages to better represent how much of a genre is a given key/mode/explicity.

In [87]:
# Creating the axes for plotting
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(15, 18))

# Creating a countplot for key distribution
sns.countplot(data=spotify_top5, x='key_string', ax=axes[0,0], order=['C', 'C♯/D♭', 'D', 'D♯/E♭', 'E', 'F', 'F♯/G♭', 'G', 'G♯/A♭', 'A', 'A♯/B♭', 'B'])
axes[0,0].set_title('Distribution of Song Keys')
axes[0,0].set_xlabel('Key')
axes[0,0].set_ylabel('Number of Songs')

.round(5)*100

axes[0,1].set_xlabel('Key')

Observations:

  • Chill: Low proportion of tracks in A key
  • Grunge: High proportion of tracks in A key, low proportion of tracks in F key
  • K-Pop: High proportion of tracks in G♯/A♭ key, high proportion of tracks with minor mode
  • Pop-Film: High proportion of tracks in C/E/G key, low proportion of tracks in C♯/D♭ key, high proportion of tracks with minor mode
  • Sad: High proportion of tracks in G♯/A♭ key, high proportion of tracks with explicity

genre_means["instrumentalness"].plot(kind="bar", ax=axes[2,1])
axes[2,1].set_title("Average Instrumentalness by Genre")
axes[2,1].set_xlabel("Genre")
axes[2,1].set_ylabel("Average Instrumentalness")

# Bar plot representing means for valence across genre
genre_means["valence"].plot(kind="bar", ax=axes[2,2])
axes[2,2].set_title("Average Valence by Genre")
axes[2,2].set_xlabel("Genre")
axes[2,2].set_ylabel("Average Valence")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observation: Here we created a summary table comparing the five audio features we chose to explore in the pop-film genre with those of the other selected genres. Through our analysis, we found that pop-film does not have one single feature that makes it stand out. Instead, the genre can be described by a combination of audio characteristics.One key observation was that pop-film generally fell in the middle of our bar graphs. None of the five features had the highest or lowest average compared with the other genres. This suggests that pop-film has a balanced combination of audio characteristics rather than being defined by one extreme feature. This balance could be an interesting direction for future research into what listeners enjoy about the genre.

Observations:

Observations regarding averages mostly follow what we have previously observed in our comparison table. Regarding our spreads:

  • Valence: Spread seems similar across genres
  • Tempo: Spread seems similar, minimum of chill and grunge are lower than other genres
  • Energy: Energy seems diverse across genres, with highest level of energy in grunge and lowest in chill. Spread seems similar but there seems to be less spread in-between the upper quartile and median.
  • Loudness: Also diverse, might be related to it being used as a measurement for energy. Grunge has a much smaller spread, and chill & sad have a wide spread.
  • Danecability: Spread seems similar; grunge has a lower minimum than the rest of the genres.
  • Liveness: Grunge has a larger spread and a higher upper quartile than other genres. It also has a higher maximum.

Conclusion¶

Using different graphing and tabling methods, we found a number of unique features that exist within each of the observed genres. A quick summary of our findings:

Chill:

  • Low % of tracks using A key
  • Low tempo, loudness, energy
  • High acousticness, instrumentalness
  • Wide spread of track values in loudness

Chill tracks seem to be unique through its features, noticeably in its low tempo and energy and high acousticness and instrumentalness. Its wide spread in loudness indicate that it is not indicative of a chill song, and chill songs can be a variety of loud.

Grunge:

  • High % of tracks using A key
  • Low % of tracks using F key
  • Low danceability, acoustic
  • High loudness, liveness, tempo
  • Narrower spread of track values in loudness
  • Wider spread of track values in liveness

Grunge tracks are unique through its high loudness, liveness, and tempo. The genre also noticeably has a low amount of danceability and acousticness. The narrow spread within loudness suggests that a specific level of loudness might be indicative for the grunge genre, and tracks within that genre mostly use the same level of loudness.

K-Pop:

  • High % of tracks using G♯/A♭ key
  • High % of tracks using minor mode
  • Low acousticness and instrumentalness
  • High valence

K-Pop tracks, like pop-film, seem to utilize minor modality much more frequently than other genres; this might suggest that a singular form of modality does not indicate that something defines whether or not a track is considered as k-pop. K-pop albums also utilize high valence while having low acousticness and instrumentalness.

Pop-Film:

  • High % of tracks using C, E, G keys
  • Low % of tracks using C♯/D♭ key
  • High % of tracks using minor mode
  • Low instrumentalness
  • High valence
  • A lot of other features' averages fall near the middle across other genres

The pop-film genre is slightly similar to K-Pop, as they both utilize minor modes, high valence, and low instrumentalness. However, we found that pop-film tracks have a high percentage of key usage within C, E, and G keys specifically; additionally, there is low usage of the C♯/D♭, which is more frequently used in other genres. Additionally, by visualizing means, we found that pop-film's feature's averages fell middle of other averages across genres.

RESEARCH QUESTION 4: What are the unique characteristics of the top 5 genres in relation to popularity?¶

When examining relationships across genres and popularity, we also became interested in how features differed based on popularity within a specific genre. To make this question conceivable given our timeframe, we split the work into 5 parts; this is discussed in the introduction. We analyse both the top 100 songs within the genre and the other songs within the genre.

The findings within this research question should be approached with caution. The samples between our top 100 and the genre as a whole is very unproportionate, and the viewer should keep this in mind when viewing any new information regarding potential differences within the top 100.

Significant features

  • Explicit: 70% of songs in the top 100 chill are not expilicit. 30% are explicit.
  • Dancibility: Dancibility is analyzed on a scale of 0.0-1.0 The mean for the top 100 chill was 0.695. This is significant and also unexpected. One might expect the opposite for the chill genre, given its name.
  • Key: Most of the songs in the top 100 chill and in the keys F and G. 52% of them to be exact.

Potentially signigicant features that need comparison with other genres

  • Speechiness: The closer a number is to 1.0 the more likely a track is exclusively speech like. The chill genre has a very low speechiness of 0.122.
  • Loudness: A score of 0 is the loudest possible. The top 100 chill scored -9.995. I am not sure of the significance because I have yet to compare with other genres and do not know the extent of the loudness scale.
  • Tempo: The same applies to tempo. I do not have a scale to gauge how slow or fast the chill genre. It also would be helpful to look at the bpm of other genres to compare.

Visual Data¶

KDE explaination: KDE is called a Kernel Dentsity Estimate. Most of the plots use KDE which is not a concept we have gone over in class. Gemini recommended it and I would like to explain why I choose to keep it in; since I am a sociology major, I have used SPSS. The KDE is very similar visually and mathmatically to the density curve used for histograms in SPSS. The KDE line in seaborn and the density curve in spss make it easy to see the peaks in the data. This makes it easier to see trends in the data and analyze

Choice of 15 bins explaination: Intially, I thought 10 bins would be ideal since that evenly splits the 100 songs. However, the data type is float which means there are decimals. Splitting into bins of 10 would eliminate/smoothe out valueable data since it may cluster them together. Because of this, 15 would be a better choice than 10.

# 10. Key Distribution (Categorical Bar Plot sorted by Pitch Class order)
#using key_map to convert the intergers to key names which I did earlier
#value_counts is used to calculate the number of times each key appears
#reindex(key_map.values() sorts the keys in the correct order accorsing to pitch
#fill_value=0 makes sure that if there is a key with no values it displays it as zero instead of dropping it
#x=key_counts.index makes it so key names are placed on the x axis
#y=key_counts.values represents number of songs in each key which is placed on the y axis
#gemini suggested adding "hue=key_counts.index" because without it I was getting a FutureWarning because of "palette=crest"
#also added "legend=False" so that the legend of colors is not displayed since it is unneecessary
#ax=axes[2, 1] is for location of graph on my grid
#palette='crest' is the gradient color palette is I am using
#set_title('Key Distribution') + set_ylabel('Song Count') are to title the graph
#tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45) rotates the key labels on the x axis by 45 degrees so that they do not overlap
key_counts = chill_genre_t100['key'].map(key_map).value_counts().reindex(key_map.values(), fill_value=0)
sns.barplot(x=key_counts.index, y=key_counts.values, hue=key_counts.index, legend=False, ax=axes[2, 1], palette='crest')
axes[2, 1].set_title('Key Distribution')
axes[2, 1].set_ylabel('Song Count')
axes[2, 1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)

# 11. Modality / Mode (Binary Bar Plot)
#in the data mode is represented by the numbers 1 and 0
#1 represents major and 0 represents minor
#map({1: 'Major', 0: 'Minor'}) converts the numbers to string so that they can be counted
#.value_counts() counts how many songs are written in major or minor
#x=mode_counts.index places major and minor on the x axis
#y=mode_counts.values places the number of songs on the y axis
#gemini suggested adding "hue=mode_counts.index" because without it I was getting a FutureWarning because of "palette=crest"
#also added "legend=False" so that the legend of colors is not displayed since it is unneecessary
#ax=axes[2, 2] positions the graph
#palette='Set2' is responsible for coloring the graph
#set_title('Modality (Major vs. Minor)'+ set_ylabel('Song Count') are to label the graph

mode_counts = chill_genre_t100['mode'].map({1: 'Major', 0: 'Minor'}).value_counts()
sns.barplot(x=mode_counts.index, y=mode_counts.values, hue=mode_counts.index, legend=False, ax=axes[2, 2], palette='Set2')
axes[2, 2].set_title('Modality (Major vs. Minor)')
axes[2, 2].set_ylabel('Song Count')

# 12.hides 12th panel grid space since its blank
axes[2, 3].axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"[DATA INFRASTRUCTURE] Total K-Pop tracks discovered in 'spotify_top5' engine: {len(kpop_all)}")

# Establish 4 empirical popularity quartiles to anchor our stratification grid
kpop_all['pop_bin'] = pd.qcut(kpop_all['popularity'], q=4, labels=['Q1_Low', 'Q2_MidLow', 'Q3_MidHigh', 'Q4_High'], duplicates='drop')

# Draw exactly 25 songs per quantile to assemble our balanced n=100 experimental dataframe
sampled_chunks = []
for name, group in kpop_all.groupby('pop_bin'):
    chunk = group.sample(n=25, random_state=42) if len(group) >= 25 else group
    sampled_chunks.append(chunk)

kpop_100 = pd.concat(sampled_chunks).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"[DATA INFRASTRUCTURE] Stratified sampling complete. Target dataframe 'kpop_100' verified: {kpop_100.shape}")

We looked at our 100-song sample to see if things like how loud or fast a song is makes it more popular on Spotify. Looking at our scatterplot graph, there is a slight correlation between loudness and correlation. However, there is still variance and may not be indicative of whether or not a song is popular. When examining this data, we should also consider variables outside of music features, like crazy fanbases streaming it on repeat to hit goals, cool dance videos, buying different versions of physical albums, and big global marketing drops.

Valence basically just means how happy or positive a song feels. In our data, the happy score is super connected to how danceable and high-energy the song is. This shows how K-Pop producers make music: they make songs sound super happy and bright by putting cheerful singing over fast, high-energy beats that are easy to dance to. But we also saw a few random dots down in the bottom-left corner. Those are the darker, sadder electronic K-Pop songs. This shows K-Pop has two sides: it balances super bright happy songs with darker, moody concepts.

K-Pop Traits and Bad Stuff About Our Data

When we took the averages for our 100 songs, we found 5 big things that make K-Pop stand out:

• Super High Energy: The songs have a ton of instruments and sound super heavy.

• Easy to Dance To: The beats are super steady because they are made for hard, synchronized choreography.

• Almost No Acoustic Sounds: K-Pop uses computer sounds and electronic synthesizers instead of real instruments like acoustic guitars.

• Lots of Talking/Rapping: Almost every K-Pop song has a rap verse or a spoken part mixed into the middle of the pop song.

• Super Loud: The music is mixed to be as loud as possible so it pops out on streaming apps.

Significant features

  • Dancibility: Dancibility is analyzed on a scale of 0.0-1.0 The mean for the top 100 sad was 0.719. This is significant and also unexpected. One might expect the opposite for the sad genre, given its name. What is even more surprising is that the dancibility is even higher than the chill genre.
  • Key: Most of the songs in the top 100 chill and in the keys G, including Gb and C#/Db. 40% of all the songs in the top 100 sad are in these keys.
  • Loudness: A score of 0 is the loudest possible. The top 100 sad scored -11.294. The sad genre has proven to be quite quiet. The sad genre is quieter than the chill genre. This is interesting because the sad genre is more quiet, yet has a higher dancibility.

# 10. Key Distribution (Categorical Bar Plot sorted by Pitch Class order)
#using key_map to convert the intergers to key names which I did earlier
#value_counts is used to calculate the number of times each key appears
#reindex(key_map.values() sorts the keys in the correct order accorsing to pitch
#fill_value=0 makes sure that if there is a key with no values it displays it as zero instead of dropping it
#x=key_counts.index makes it so key names are placed on the x axis
#y=key_counts.values represents number of songs in each key which is placed on the y axis
#gemini suggested adding "hue=key_counts.index" because without it I was getting a FutureWarning because of "palette=rocket"
#also added "legend=False" so that the legend of colors is not displayed since it is unneecessary
#ax=axes[2, 1] is for location of graph on my grid
#palette='crest' is the gradient color palette is I am using
#set_title('Key Distribution') + set_ylabel('Song Count') are to title the graph
#tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45) rotates the key labels on the x axis by 45 degrees so that they do not overlap
key_counts = sad_genre['key'].map(key_map).value_counts().reindex(key_map.values(), fill_value=0)
sns.barplot(x=key_counts.index, y=key_counts.values, hue=key_counts.index, legend=False, ax=axes[2, 1], palette='rocket')
axes[2, 1].set_title('Key Distribution')
axes[2, 1].set_ylabel('Song Count')
axes[2, 1].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)

# 11. Modality / Mode (Binary Bar Plot)
#in the data mode is represented by the numbers 1 and 0
#1 represents major and 0 represents minor
#map({1: 'Major', 0: 'Minor'}) converts the numbers to string so that they can be counted
#.value_counts() counts how many songs are written in major or minor
#x=mode_counts.index places major and minor on the x axis
#y=mode_counts.values places the number of songs on the y axis
#gemini suggested adding "hue=mode_counts.index" because without it I was getting a FutureWarning because of "palette=set3"
#also added "legend=False" so that the legend of colors is not displayed since it is unneecessary
#ax=axes[2, 2] positions the graph
#palette='Set2' is responsible for coloring the graph
#set_title('Modality (Major vs. Minor)'+ set_ylabel('Song Count') are to label the graph

mode_counts = sad_genre['mode'].map({1: 'Major', 0: 'Minor'}).value_counts()
sns.barplot(x=mode_counts.index, y=mode_counts.values, hue=mode_counts.index, legend=False, ax=axes[2, 2], palette='Set3')
axes[2, 2].set_title('Modality (Major vs. Minor)')
axes[2, 2].set_ylabel('Song Count')

# 12.hides 12th panel grid space since its blank
axes[2, 3].axis('off')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

PROJECT 1: KEY DISCOVERIES AND TAKEAWAYS¶

Discoveries on Popularity¶

  1. Variance in summary statistics of numerical features across groups
  2. Proportional differences in categorical features
  3. Visual differences when graphing and comparing data

Valence Relationships¶

  1. Weak, positive correlation between valence and loudness, energy, danceability

Genre Characteristics¶

  1. Unique findings regarding means and spreads (IQR) when comparing across genres
  2. Certain genres had unique proportional differences when examining categorical data

Popularity Findings within Genres¶

  1. Correlations discovered through graphical data (i.e. scatterplot)
  2. More informative approach used within some genres, aiming to analyze within the top 100 instead of comparison
  3. Potential insight towards the role the amount of songs an artist creates adds towards popularity

Data Science Insights¶

  • Different methods, especially when examining numerical versus categorical data, helps uncover informational data regarding differences across groups
  • Visualization and tabling are both necessary in our process
  • Serendipitous discoveries can be made through data science (ex. a large proportion of songs in a minor mode within pop) -- we don't know everything

Why Our Work Matters¶

Our information would prove useful to enhance recommendation systems on Spotify when it comes to genres. The system would be able to more accurately predict new genres that listeners may be interested in.
